{{Short description|Weather forecast phenomenon}}
'''Wet bias''' is the phenomenon whereby some [[weather forecasting|weather forecasters]] report an overestimated and exaggerated probability of [[precipitation]] to increase the usefulness and actionability of their forecast.<ref name=nytimes>{{cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2012/09/09/magazine/the-weatherman-is-not-a-moron.html?pagewanted=all&_r=0|title = The Weatherman Is Not a Moron|last = Silver|first = Nate|author-link = Nate Silver|date = September 7, 2012|access-date = May 24, 2014|newspaper = [[New York Times]]}}</ref><ref name=wapo>{{cite news|url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/blogs/wonkblog/wp/2012/09/27/why-everyone-hates-the-weatherman/|title = Why everyone hates the weatherman| newspaper=[[The Washington Post]] |date = September 27, 2012|access-date = May 24, 2014}}</ref><ref name=danallan>{{cite web|url = http://blog.danallan.com/notes/2012/wet-bias/|title = Wet Bias|last = Allan|first = Dan|access-date = May 24, 2014|archive-date = February 7, 2014|archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20140207120907/http://blog.danallan.com/notes/2012/wet-bias/|url-status = dead}}</ref> [[The Weather Channel]] has been empirically shown, and has also admitted, to having a wet bias in the case of low probability of precipitation (for instance, a 5% probability may be reported as a 20% probability) but not at high probabilities of precipitation (so a 60% probability will be reported as a 60% probability). Some [[Local programming|local television stations]] have been shown as having significantly greater wet bias, often reporting a 100% probability of precipitation in cases where it rains only 70% of the time.<ref name=nytimes/><ref name=signal-noise/>

==Discovery==
In 2002, Eric Floehr, a computer science graduate of the [[Ohio State University]], started collecting historical data of weather forecasts made by the [[National Weather Service]] (NWS), [[The Weather Channel]] (TWC), and [[AccuWeather]] for the United States, and collected the data on ForecastWatch.com.<ref name=signal-noise>{{cite book|last = Silver|first = Nate|title = The Signal and the Noise: Why So Many Prediction Fail|isbn = 978-1594204111|title-link = The Signal and the Noise|year = 2012}}, Page 131-136</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://forecastwatch.com/|title = ForecastWatch: Accuracy Defined|access-date = May 24, 2014}}</ref> Floehr found that the commercial forecasts were biased: they consistently predicted a higher probability of precipitation than actually occurred. The NWS forecasts were unbiased, whereas those at The Weather Channel were biased for low probabilities of precipitation: when TWC predicted a 20% probability of precipitation, it had historically rained only 5% of the time, but a 70% probability of precipitation corresponded with the real rate of precipitation.<ref name=nytimes/><ref name=signal-noise/><ref>{{cite journal|title = Verification of The Weather Channel Probability of Precipitation Forecasts|last1 = Bickel|first1 = Eric|last2 = Dae Kim|first2 = Seong|doi = 10.1175/2008MWR2547.1|journal = [[Monthly Weather Review]]|volume = 136|pages = 4867–4881|issue = 12|date = December 2008|bibcode = 2008MWRv..136.4867B|citeseerx = 10.1.1.558.1663}}</ref><ref name=forecastadvisor-twc>{{cite web|url=http://www.forecastadvisor.com/blog/2012/09/19/icon_forecast_bias_surprises/|title = Icon Forecast Bias and Pleasant Surprises|publisher = ForecastAdvisor|date = September 19, 2012|access-date = May 24, 2014}}</ref> Blogger Dan Allan noted that The Weather Channel is also biased at the upper end: a probability of 90% or higher will be rounded up to 100%.<ref name=danallan/> On the other hand, local television stations tended to exaggerate the probability of precipitation throughout (except when they forecast a probability of 0%, in which case it still rained about 10% of the time).<ref name=signal-noise/> The findings on wet bias, though informally well known within the weather forecasting community for some time, were first popularized outside the weather forecasting community in [[Nate Silver]]'s 2012 book ''[[The Signal and the Noise]]''.<ref name=signal-noise/>

The term ''wet bias'' is used because this is a [[systematic bias]] in the direction of the weather being wetter than it actually is.

==Reasons for wet bias==
According to Silver, The Weather Channel has openly admitted to deliberately exaggerating the probability of precipitation when it is low. This is because of biased incentives: if the correct low probability of precipitation is given, viewers may interpret the forecast as if there were no probability of rain, and then be upset if it does rain. In other words, The Weather Channel compensates for inaccurate perceptions of probabilities. Silver quotes Dr. Rose of The Weather Channel as saying, "If the forecast was objective, if it has zero bias in precipitation, we are in trouble."<ref name=nytimes/><ref name=signal-noise/><ref name=forecastadvisor-twc/>
